wumen.name: Wumen Gate

items.title: Throne and screen
items.text: The dragon-carved throne stands on a raised platform, with a seven-panel screen behind it and a separate footstool in front. Palace Museum records state that, after the throne was rediscovered in storage, its restoration took more than a year and was completed in September 1964.

items.title: The Jianji Suiyou plaque
items.text: The original Jianji Suiyou plaque above the throne, whose inscription concerns establishing the highest standard and bringing peace through good governance, bore Qianlong's calligraphy. A 2002 Palace Museum record states that the original plaque's whereabouts were unknown. The plaque and paired inscriptions were therefore reproduced using a photograph from 1900 and returned to their positions on 18 September that year.

items.title: Caisson ceiling and pearls
items.text: Above and in front of the throne, the caisson ceiling narrows in stages from a square to an octagon and a circle. A carved dragon in the center lowers its head. Official photographs show a group of one large and six small spheres, surrounded by a coffered ceiling decorated with dragons.

items.title: Six golden columns
items.text: Six large golden columns stand on the two sides of the throne. Their cloud-and-dragon designs are built up in shallow relief using raised paste decoration, then covered with two shades of gold leaf to make the dragons stand out against the golden ground.

items.title: Four pairs of objects before the throne
items.text: On either side in front of the throne are paired elephants, luduan mythical beasts, cranes and pavilion-shaped incense holders. The elephants carry vases, and the cranes have slender necks and legs. The incense pavilions belong to the pavilion-shaped incense-container type, distinct from ding-shaped incense burners.

items.title: A main hall for grand ceremonies
items.text: Taihe Hall was mainly used for major ceremonies such as enthronements, empress investitures and festival congratulations. Emperors had separate sleeping quarters for everyday life; Ming emperors, for example, lived in Qianqing Palace. The throne here should be understood in its ceremonial setting.

timeline.text: Originally named Huagai Hall, then Zhongji Hall; renamed Zhonghe Hall in the early Qing dynasty.
